claude.sample_unit: clinicians (each diagnosing 200 ACL MRIs with and without AI)
models_evaluated: ACL rupture diagnosis AI on MRI

links.outcome: Clinician diagnostic accuracy with versus without AI assistance; automation bias share of errors
links.effect: AI increased clinician accuracy from 87.2%±13.1% to 96.4%±1.9% (P<.001); automation bias accounted for 45.5% of errors in AI-assisted round.
links.quote: The AI significantly increased clinicians' accuracy from 87.2%±13.1% to 96.4%±1.9% (P < .001).

links.outcome: Proportion of clinician errors attributable to automation bias, across expertise levels
links.effect: Clinicians' errors in AI-assisted round associated with automation bias accounted for 45.5% of total mistakes; affected clinicians of all expertise levels.
links.quote: However, the clinicians' errors in the AI-assisted round were associated with automation bias, accounting for 45.5% of the total mistakes.

links.outcome: Estimated reduction in automation bias from suppressing AI outputs in high misleading-probability zone
links.effect: Proposed AI suppression strategy was estimated to decrease clinicians' automation bias by 41.7%.
links.quote: The proposed AI suppression strategy was estimated to decrease clinicians' automation bias by 41.7%.

unlisted_practices: Suppressing AI diagnoses in output zones with higher predicted misleading probability using ordinal logistic regression

screen.practice: AI output suppression / selective withholding of AI suggestions to reduce automation bias
screen.reason: The study tests an AI suppression strategy (selectively withholding AI recommendations predicted to have high risk of misleading clinicians) to mitigate automation bias in clinician MRI evaluation.
